new_statements.quote: The prosodic features of Lealao Chinantec are length, ballistic accent, and tone. [...] 3.1. Length and accent. The features of vocalic length and accent have developed quite regularly from the ancestor language. [fn:] Compare Rensch and Rensch (1966:456f) for a somewhat different treatment of a similar phenomenon. For reasons of distribution, the ballistic accent is there analyzed as the postnuclear variant of /h/, which apparently is its source in Proto Otomanguean (Rensch 1976, §9.2.3). [p. 87:] Tone /2/ in syllables bearing the ballistic accent has a variant which falls sharply, as is characteristic of accented syllables (Rupp 1990).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog (which has an entry for the language with no rule) and with Rupp 1990: it adds that the 'ballistic accent' is a lexical, etymological feature (from *h) layered on the tone system, not a positional word stress. Note: the catalog's open_url (sil.org/resources/archives/8586) is the WRONG item ('Phonemic systems of Colombian languages'); the correct SIL record is archives/8501 (PDF, could not be reached by automated download live; found via the SIL OAI dump). The article was read from the whole-volume PDF (SIL archives/8897, Internet Archive copy 2017-12-12); the scan has no text layer, so pages were scanned with tesseract at 150 dpi.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A diachronic paper: it lists the prosodic features of Lealao as length, ballistic accent and tone (four tones /1 2 3 4/), treats the ballistic accent as a lexical property of the syllable inherited regularly from Proto-Chinantec (ultimately Proto-Otomanguean *-h, cognate with syllable-final /h/ in Lalana), and says nothing about where word stress falls; for the synchronic stress placement it defers to Rupp 1990.
new_statements.exceptions: None about placement. A footnote on p. 78 speculates that *tiV became dyV 'under obscure conditions, perhaps that of weakened stress'.
new_statements.identity_note: Rupp's data are from San Juan Lealao, Oaxaca (with additional speakers in Latani and Santa María Yahuivé), collected 1968-1980s with three named native speakers (fn. 1, p. 63); Rensch's Lealao forms were supplied by Rupp (fn. 1, p. 75). The dictionary sketch (Rupp & Rupp 1996, p. 388) notes that the Ozumacín variety differs in keeping i-diphthongs after velars, but says nothing about a stress difference between varieties.

new_statements.quote: The phonological word is typically just one stressed syllable, although a verb may be realized phonologically as a string of as many as six syllables. The stressed syllable is the last syllable of the word unless the word ends with one of five unstressed person markers. [...] There are two kinds of stress, ballistic and controlled. A ballistic syllable (marked by an acute accent /´/ over the nuclear vowel of the syllable) is shorter than a controlled one (correspondingly marked by a grave accent /`/), and is characterized by a rapid decrease in loudness and lowering in pitch. [p. 64:] Apart from lack of stress, unstressed syllables differ from stressed syllables only in their relative simplicity.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has Lealao Chinantec with an empty rule (qs-tier-2026-09-12) and no existing statements; this work supplies the placement rule (final syllable, minus unstressed person-marker suffixes) and the ballistic/controlled stress-type contrast. The scan has no text layer; the accent-mark glyphs inside the slashes were garbled by scanned and are restored here as /´/ and /`/ per the running text. Data from San Juan Lealao (fn. 1). The catalog's open_url (sil.org/resources/archives/8585) is the right record but its PDF is could not be reached by automated download and has no archived copy at the Internet Archive; the chapter was read from the whole-volume PDF.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word has exactly one stressed syllable, the last syllable of the word, except that when the word ends in one of five unstressed person-marker suffixes the stress stays on the syllable before them (i.e. on the stem; pretonic prefix syllables such as the future marker are also unstressed). Stressed syllables come in two lexically contrasting types, 'ballistic' (short, sharp fall in loudness and pitch, written with an acute) and 'controlled' (written with a grave). Only stressed syllables allow consonant clusters, length, nasalization and tone sequences; unstressed syllables carry only a single tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'a unit constituted of syllables of which only one is stressed' (p. 63). Unstressed pretonic and posttonic syllables may carry any single tone but not tone sequences (p. 72). A posttonic person marker may be lexically marked for ballistic stress, and then triggers tone sandhi in the preceding stressed syllable, although it is itself pronounced without stress (p. 72).
new_statements.exceptions: Words ending in one of five unstressed person markers (person suffixes), e.g. the first-singular and first-plural-inclusive markers, which are posttonic; the stressed syllable is then the one before the marker.
new_statements.identity_note: Rupp's data are from San Juan Lealao, Oaxaca (with additional speakers in Latani and Santa María Yahuivé), collected 1968-1980s with three named native speakers (fn. 1, p. 63); Rensch's Lealao forms were supplied by Rupp (fn. 1, p. 75). The dictionary sketch (Rupp & Rupp 1996, p. 388) notes that the Ozumacín variety differs in keeping i-diphthongs after velars, but says nothing about a stress difference between varieties.

new_statements.quote: There are also two articles relating to Lealao Chinantec, the subject of volume 2 of this subseries, both predating the latter in writing. Rensch's manuscript, placing Lealao data within the context of his comparative work on Proto-Chinantec phonology, was originally drafted in close association with the syllable paper that appears here with it. [Rupp, p. 63:] Stress, length, nasalization, and tone are prominent features of the Lealao Chinantec syllable, as is true of other Chinantec languages. The syllable is a constituent of the phonological word, a unit constituted of syllables of which only one is stressed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The edited volume itself (the MPI handle record) is the container of works 1 and 2; its Lealao content is Rupp's syllable paper (one stressed syllable per word, the last unless a person-marker suffix follows) and Rensch's diachronic paper. The remaining chapters concern Comaltepec Chinantec tone and verb inflection (Anderson, Martinez & Pace; Pace), Quiotepec Chinantec tone (Gardner & Merrifield) and Tepetotutla Chinantec motion verbs (Westley & Merrifield), not this language.
new_statements.secondary_stress: As in work 2: none; only one stressed syllable per phonological word.
new_statements.exceptions: As in work 2: five unstressed word-final person markers.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages are verbatim on the page images we hold of Rupp 1989 pp.1 and 3 (PDF pp.15,17) and the ms p.1 (PDF p.2), at the stated locators. (2) The classification rests on the language's only reference grammar (Rupp 1989, phonology chapter) by the principal fieldworker, plus his syllable paper draft; the classification 'morphological: root stress, up to five unstressed prefix syllables, at most one unstressed person-marker after the root; ballistic/controlled is a lexical stress-type contrast on that syllable' is exactly what p.1, p.3 and the ms say. (3) Newly downloaded Rupp & Rupp 1996 dictionary grammar (120-pp sketch) treats only 'acento balístico' (0.5, p.388) and presupposes unstressed suffixes after the root (p.386); it is silent on placement and contradicts nothing. No instrumental or later phonological study of Lealao stress surfaced in Semantic Scholar/CrossRef/S
